chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
I asked him about the dower (mahr), so he said: 'Whatever the people agree upon, or twelve awqiya and one nashsh, or five hundred dirhams.'

key_terms.أُوقِيَّةً: A unit of weight/currency, plural awqiya
key_terms.الْمَهْرِ: Dower or bridal gift given by the husband to the wife
key_terms.دِرْهَمٍ: A silver coin, unit of currency
key_terms.نَشًّا: A smaller unit of weight/currency, often a fraction of an awqiya

ai.seo_question: What is the prescribed amount for the Islamic dower (mahr) according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) establishes that the dower (mahr) is primarily governed by mutual consent (taradhi), reflecting the flexibility of Shia jurisprudence, while citing twelve awqiya and one nashsh (or five hundred dirhams) as the traditional benchmark for a 'moderate' or standard amount. This hadith highlights the distinction between the legal validity of any agreed-upon sum and the cultural norm of a reasonable default, a principle widely accepted by Shia jurists to prevent both exploitation and excessive burden. The reference to specific coinage anchors the concept in the economic context of the early Islamic period, providing a tangible baseline for contemporary scholarly calculations of mahr value.
